body: Above a dental clinic in a Japanese city, on the second floor of the building and next to a stairwell that smells faintly of the ramen place downstairs, a congregation is meeting on Sunday morning. Shoes are lined up by the door. There is a folding keyboard, a projector aimed at a slightly crooked screen, and a rice cooker in the corner for afterwards. Eleven people are there, one of them a student who came because a friend asked twice. The pastor teaches English during the week, because the offering does not come close to a stipend, and everybody knows it and nobody mentions it.

No version of that morning shows up in a report. It is too small to register, and it will be too small next year, and the year after. And it is the visible end of one of the most extraordinary survival stories the Christian faith has anywhere on earth.

Christianity in Japan is a very small minority — small enough that the figure is usually the only thing anybody hears about it, and small enough that the conversation tends to stop there, with a shrug about hard soil.

The title of this piece puts two words next to each other that we do not normally allow together, and it is worth sitting with the discomfort for a moment. Tiny and old. We assume without noticing that a small church is a young church — a plant not grown yet, a mission in its early stages, something at the start of a curve that will bend upwards if it is watered properly. Every metaphor we reach for is agricultural and every one implies time is on our side. Japan will not fit that. This is not a church that has not grown yet. It is one that has been there for centuries, that was once considerably larger, that was hunted almost out of existence and did not go, and that has been small for longer than most denominations have existed. Small and old at once. Our vocabulary has no slot for it.

This dial carries 40 international stations in 29 languages, hosted in those languages rather than translated into them afterwards. One of them is HM 336.60 — Japan Inspire, in Japanese, anchored in Tokyo with relays in Los Angeles and Honolulu, and it is on air today.

It will have the smallest audience on the band and everyone involved knew that when the number was assigned. A frequency here belongs to one station permanently and cannot be recycled, so HM 336.60 is a commitment that will never be justified by its listener figures, made in a stretch of dial where a larger language could have been put. It is held anyway, and not out of sentimentality about small things. The history behind this particular small thing makes the usual way of counting look ridiculous.

The history, in outline, is not disputed. The faith arrived in the middle of the sixteenth century with missionaries from Europe and it did not creep. It spread fast, particularly in the south and around Nagasaki, among farmers and fishermen and some of the nobility. Then the authorities turned, and the turn was thorough. Missionaries were expelled. Christians were executed publicly and deliberately, some of them crucified on a hillside above the harbour at Nagasaki, Japanese and European together, the ordained alongside labourers and children. The intention was to demonstrate rather than merely to punish, and as a demonstration it worked. Then the country closed, and the door stayed shut a very long time.

What followed was administrative rather than dramatic, which is what made it effective. Households were required to prove they were not Christian by treading on a bronze image of Christ or of his mother — a small object, brought round, in front of neighbours, on a scheduled day. Renunciation was made into paperwork, which may be the most efficient instrument of suppression anybody has devised: it needs no court and no execution, only a doorstep and an audience.
By every measure available at the time, the mission to Japan had failed completely.

It is worth being fair to that judgement, because it was not stupid. There was nobody left to lead. The buildings were gone or converted, the missionaries dead or deported, the books destroyed, the practice criminal, the country sealed. Any reasonable observer would have written the account off and moved the resources somewhere they might do good, and that is not greed but stewardship, applied in every mission committee on earth every year. But notice what such a judgement cannot see. It cannot see a thing that has stopped growing and has not stopped existing. It has no category for faith that is being transmitted with none of the equipment that transmission is supposed to require, and so it records a zero, and the zero is wrong.
Because the communities did not go. They went down.

The nineteenth century opens the door a crack, and a church is built at Nagasaki, meant for foreign residents rather than for anybody local. A French priest is there. One afternoon a group of villagers comes in and stands about, looking, the way people do in a new building. A woman moves close to him and says, quietly, that the heart of all of us here is the same as his. Then she asks him where the statue of Mary is. She is not asking for instruction and she is not converting. She is checking whether this man is one of theirs, and the question about the image is the test, because the image is what her people kept when everything else was taken.

For roughly two centuries there were no priests, no Bibles and no buildings, and when the doors finally opened the faith was still there. What had carried it was the least impressive machinery imaginable: prayers said aloud from memory until the words wore smooth and stopped being Latin or Portuguese or anything anyone could parse, baptism performed by laymen and by women, a calendar of feasts kept in secret, and objects that looked to a passing official like something else entirely.

There is no triumphal ending here and it would be dishonest to write one. Not everybody came back. When the priests returned, some of those communities looked at the church on offer and decided, after generations of doing it themselves, that what they had was what their fathers handed them and they would keep it as it was. Their descendants are distinct still, and their practice is fading now in a way persecution never managed. The church in Japan has not surged since. It remains small, and the station will not change that.

Which is the point, and it only works if the ending stays unresolved. If the story finished with a revival, it would be a story about growth, and we already have a thousand of those and they are all being used to argue that faithfulness pays. This one argues something harder and more useful: that a church can be small for four hundred years and still be there, that survival is a legitimate outcome, and that everything we count was invisible to the people doing the keeping. Nobody treading around a bronze plate in a village yard was building a movement. They were getting through one more inspection, and then another, and that turned out to be enough.

So a station in Japanese, on a dial that could have spent the frequency on a language with far more speakers behind it, is not charity and it is not a gesture. It is an admission that the size of a thing tells you almost nothing about its weight, and that the church which took the worst treatment on record and simply endured it deserves a number of its own on the band, permanently, whether or not anybody is listening tonight.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing.

The dial carries four kinds of programming — music, which is most of the band; teaching and prayer; family programming; and the international stations. The Asian stretch of the international band has plenty still to come: Korea Inspire at HM 335.20, Indonesia Inspire at HM 338.30, Bengal Inspire at HM 333.80, all assigned, all in build, none on air yet. Several of their neighbours are already up, and one of them is the reason you have read this far.

Put on HM 336.60 — Japan Inspire. It is on air now. It runs in Japanese, gentle worship and contemplative teaching, with morning praise at seven and evening worship at eight, on Tokyo time, and relays into Los Angeles and Honolulu that carry it across the date line for the diaspora. If you do not speak Japanese, put it on anyway, and give it a quarter of an hour rather than a polite thirty seconds. You will follow almost none of it. You will pick out a tune you know under words you do not, and you will hear a room addressed in the language it actually thinks in, which is the whole reason these stations are hosted rather than dubbed. Fifteen minutes of not being the audience is a small thing to ask on behalf of the people in this article.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, wherever they are. Add the page to your home screen if you like. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band finds out which languages people are reaching for, which is how the ones still in build get their opening dates.

So take it as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not evaluate the station, because you are not equipped to and neither am I. Put HM 336.60 on this evening while you are doing something else and let it play in a language you do not speak, and consider, while it is on, that the people it is made for are the descendants of a church that kept going for two centuries with nothing at all. They had no frequency and no book. They had a memorised prayer and a neighbour who knew, and that turned out to be sufficient — which ought to encourage anybody who has ever felt that what they are holding on to is much too small to matter.
